title: The three left behind
hook: three men who stayed from Tabuk are forgiven after long waiting because they told the truth (9:118)
carry: the earth felt narrow, then wide

segments.voice: Yesterday, a mosque founded on piety, built on taqwa from the first day. Your line was founded on piety. When you checked why you were building something, what did you find? Day four hundred twenty-five.

Dawn, in Medina. A man is praying the morning prayer on the roof of his house, alone. For fifty nights, no one in the city has spoken to him. Then, from the top of a hill called Sal', a voice shouts, as loud as it can: Ka'b ibn Malik, good news! He falls down in prostration. You met Ka'b last year, on the day he told the Prophet ﷺ the plain truth: he had no excuse for staying home from Tabuk. Today we read the verse that ended his waiting, and what the waiting was like from the inside.

Ka'b tells the waiting himself, in Bukhari and Muslim. His two companions in it, Murara and Hilal, stayed home and wept. Ka'b, the youngest, kept going out. He prayed in the mosque, greeted the Prophet, and watched to see if his lips moved in reply. Then a letter came, from the king of Ghassan, a Christian Arab ruler allied with Byzantium: we hear your master has shunned you; come to us, and we'll honor you. Ka'b read it and said: this too is a test. And he threw it into an oven. An open door to comfort, and he burned it. Then verse one hundred eighteen came down. In paraphrase: God turned also to the three who were left behind, when the earth, vast as it is, became narrow for them, and their own souls became narrow, and they knew there was no refuge from God except in Him. Then He turned to them, so that they could turn. Notice the order. God turns first; then they turn. The verse before it, one hundred seventeen, says God had already turned to the Prophet and to those who marched with him in the hour of hardship, after some of their hearts had nearly swerved. So the three aren't set apart as the only ones who needed mercy. They're placed in the same sentence as everyone who went. And verse one hundred nineteen closes it: be with the truthful. When Ka'b came to the Prophet that morning, his face was shining. Ka'b offered to give away all his wealth; he was told to keep some. And he vowed that, since the truth had saved him, he would speak only the truth for the rest of his life.
screen: `A KING'S LETTER, INTO THE OVEN.` · `THE EARTH, VAST, GREW NARROW.` · `GOD TURNS FIRST; THEN THEY TURN.` · `BE WITH THE TRUTHFUL.` · then, large: `THE EARTH FELT NARROW, THEN WIDE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wait honestly for forgiveness. Sit, and breathe. Bring to mind something you got wrong, where you're still waiting: for someone to answer, to soften, to trust you again. Notice the narrowness of it. Notice, too, any easy way out that's being offered, a story that would make it not your fault. Don't take it. Just wait, honestly, for these two minutes. If you pray, you can turn toward God with it, the way the three did, with nowhere else to go. The bell holds the time.
The three left behind. Ka'b, Murara and Hilal, who told the truth about Tabuk, waited fifty nights, and were turned to by God in 9:118. Today's word.
Your line: the earth felt narrow, then wide. Today, if something offers you an easy way out of an honest wait, notice it, and leave it in the oven. Day four hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: The story of Ka'b ibn Malik is taught at length in Muslim study circles as a lesson in honesty and repentance, and 9:118–119 are recited as a reminder that God turns toward people so that they can turn back, and to be with the truthful.

original.note: Arabic: "the earth, vast as it is, became narrow for them" (9:118).

trapdoor: what you thought: three men punished for skipping a battle.
what it means: three men who refused to lie, waited in silence, and were turned to by God, who turns first.
what a scholar hears: 9:118 uses the same verb, taba, for God turning and for the three turning back; 9:117 includes the Prophet, the Muhajirun and the Ansar in the same divine turning.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 4418; Sahih Muslim 2769 (Ka'b ibn Malik's account)

notes: Year 1 day 282 told the confession scene; this day takes the waiting, the king's letter and 9:117–119 instead.

Details from Ka'b's account (the letter from the king of Ghassan, burning it in an oven, the call from Mount Sal', prostration, his shining face, the offer to give away his wealth, the vow of truthfulness) from memory of Bukhari 4418 / Muslim 2769; confirm.
Describing the king of Ghassan as a Christian Arab ruler allied with Byzantium: confirm.
'Forty-some days' in the fork follows the account's timing (the letter came before the fortieth day in most tellings); confirm or simplify.
